speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the speech from the throne and had opportunity to digest it somewhat, we notice several things in it that might be debated. I am not going to take time to go through the speech from beginning to end, but coming to those parts which refer to the wheat board and the royal commission on grain marketing and its effect upon the grain exchanges, also the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, I was immediately reminded of what happened at the last session of parliament with regard to some of these matters. I suppose that on account of the prospective visit of their majesties to Canada this year it will be the desire of the house to hasten its business as much as possible in order that prorogation may be reached before the time of their majesties' visit. Last session there was ample time to
The Address-Mr. Hansell

conclude in good time for his excellency to have prorogued parliament himself. I have referred to one or two items in the speech from the throne because some of these items were left until the dying days of the last session.
I might take a moment to review the business of this house at the last session. It will be recalled that the budget was considerably delayed, the reason given, and perhaps it was a legitimate one, being that the Canada-United States trade agreement was expected to be brought down at any time. Day after day, week after week it was about to come, but at last budget day was announced and the trade agreement did not come down. We all know what happened. I am certain that if we had waited for the trade agreement to be consummated, we would have had to stay here several months later than wc did. However that is past and gone.
The report of the grain commission was brought down in this house on May 9. The appropriate item under which the report could be discussed was not brought down by the minister until June 30, the day on which it was expected parliament would prorogue. His excellency had arranged passage and was to sail on July 1. Many of us wanted to speak on the grain commission report, but it would have been very unpopular for us to have taken time to make our speeches when the whole house was expecting parliament to prorogue perhaps within a few hours. We all know the result. One hon. member from the government side spoke upon the report at length, and one hon. member from the Conservative party spoke on it; those two men were quite capable of speaking on it, and the rest of us felt that in order to facilitate the business of the house we should refrain from speaking. But some of us felt that it was rather unfair for this particular item to be brought down on the last day of parliament, when it could have been brought down several weeks before.
That day, June 30, wore on. and it was almost midnight when the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) brought down some of his estimates. I have particular reference now to the estimate for subventions on coal, some $2,250,000. That estimate *was brought down toward midnight of June 30. The subject of coal mining is of great interest to many hon. members, those from Nova Scotia and Alberta perhaps in particular. It was going on to midnight; parliament was expected to prorogue at any minute, maybe at one or two or three o'clock in the

morning, and the whole house was continually crying. "Carried", "Carried", "Carried", when an item of this kind was still to be discussed. Such items as this are of tremendous importance. Nova Scotia has a coal mining industry which is very important to that province, and the same is true of Alberta. Ample time should be given for discussion of these matters. Of course I know it will be said that there is no desire to shut off discussion, but we all know how unpopular it is for one to take time to speak in those dying hours of the session when everyone wants to get away. Subsequently to that, along towards midnight the Minister of Alines and Resources brought down his estimates for highways. Some hon. members no doubt recall those particular estimates, and it is a singular fact that the appropriations to the provinces involved amounts from $100,000 to $500,000, except that the amount for Alberta was $75,000. The former leader of the opposition characterised that as being a punishment for Alberta rather than a reward. It is singular that such an estimate should be left until the very dying hours of the session.
I go a little further. That night we adjourned at twenty minutes after midnight, at which time there were still important estimates to be dealt with; estimates of the defence department; an amount of three and a half million dollars for rehabilitation; the estimates for the youth training program, and estimates concerning unemployment relief. On July 1 we assembled at 10.30 o'clock in the morning, and a message was read by you, Mr. Speaker, from his excellency's secretary, saying that the deputy of his excellency would proceed to the senate chamber at one o'clock to prorogue parliament. Still we had those very, very important items to consider. At 12.30 o'clock, about half an hour before the time set for prorogation, the estimate providing 83,-
500.000	for rehabilitation was brought before the committee. As we all know, one does not become very popular if one speaks at length when everyone is anxious to get away, but the item respecting rehabilitation was an important matter, concerning the drought area of the west, most of which lies in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The peculiar thing about the matter, as far as some of us are concerned, is that there is no reason why such an estimate could not have been brought down very early in the session in order to provide ample opportunity for discussion. However, to resume, we adjourned at one o'clock and came back at three o'clock in the afternoon to continue the discussion on the rehabilitation estimate. The estimate for the

The Address-Mrs. Black
youth training program, amounting to more than a million dollars, still had to be discussed.
I am pointing out these matters because some of us felt that it was not altogether fair to us to have these estimates left until the last hours of the session. We do not wish to imply that this was done on purpose, but it is certain that these particular items were of tremendous importance to this country and should have been far more generally discussed. We want to facilitate the business of parliament; but no one can further the business of this house better than those who sit on the treasury benches, and we would ask that during this session some of these important items be brought forward in the not too far distant future in order that they may be adequately discussed. We feel that, without becoming too unpopular, we should have an opportunity to discuss these matters. We do not want to put our request in the form of a warning, but we do want to urge that these estimates be brought down early.
There are other points that we might mention in connection with the speech from the throne. I might recall that the Liberal party went into power on that glorious promise of reforming the money policy of this country, based on the theory of issuing currency and credit in terms of public need. By this time that statement has been worn almost threadbare. It is to be noticed that in the speech from the throne this year such policies are conspicuous by their absence. This year nothing is said about doing anything in the way of monetary reform. Well, perhaps it has all been done; perhaps the battle that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) promised to fight has been finished. We did not notice any smoke in the air; but perhaps if there was any it has been all cleared away, and the country cannot expect any more. However, I would not place too much reliance upon the fact that this subject is not mentioned in the speech from the throne, because it will be recalled that last year the speech from the throne contained nothing with regard to monetary reform; yet some time around the middle or towards the latter part of the session the Prime Minister was pleased to bring down a bill providing for the purchase of all the stock of the Bank of Canada. So perhaps a good deal of our legislation depends upon the political pulse of the country. I do not know, but last year's experience would seem to indicate that.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we in this corner of the house are somewhat disappointed that there is no reference in the speech from the throne
to money reform. We have continually urged upon the government that the only solution to the problems of this country is a positive readjustment of our money policy. Nothing is being done. How much longer must we urge that action be taken? Perhaps the best we can expect is that the next time the people have an opportunity to speak they will speak in a voice that can be understood.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my word of congratulation to the mover and the seponder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Especially do I wish to congratulate that younger member, the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier). It has been my good fortune to know the hon. gentleman rather well, and when I see a young man speaking with equal facility in both French and English I am really consumed with envy. Ever since I have lived in this country, which has been for forty years now, and have known it as a bilingual country, I have felt it a shame that the young people of this day and age, as of forty years ago, have not been taught to speak both French and English. We have in the hon. member for Stormont a shining example of what the young people of to-day should know.
Perhaps it is unnecessary for me to touch upon the trade agreement. More and more as I come here each session I have a feeling of isolation; I feel more and more that I am alone. It is not that every individual member is not exceedingly kind and courteous; it is because of the fact that my constituency is so isolated and so far away from the rest of Canada. The trade agreement affects us not at all. In that north land we produce only the mediums of exchange, namely, gold and silver. When times are prosperous in Canada-or, as we in the north call it, on the outside-we pay higher prices for the goods we purchase. When depression is rampant throughout the country we are able to get our goods for less. So I think hon. members will understand when I say that from a selfish standpoint the trade agreement affects us not at all.
It seems to me that we on this continent are singularly blessed in the peace that we have, outwardly at least, throughout the country. We are free to use our own language. We are free to worship in whatever church we choose. We are free to move about whither we will. There is no one to say us nay, no one to regiment us as the peoples of Europe are regimented. I have been both shocked and surprised in reading papers throughout Canada
The Address-Mrs. Black

to see that other people are demanding the rights of -their languages. I have not been afraid that either this government or any future government will listen to those demands, because any government must have before it the horrible example of the continent of Europe, with its multiplicity of languages, which has become a modern tower of Babel. That factor must account for much of the trouble taking place in Europe at the present time.
During the September crisis we in the Yukon heard the voice of the world over the radio. We were thousands of miles from London, the heart of empire; yet there was not a heart in the Yukon but beat in unison with the tragedy which was taking place overseas. There was no one who did not feel the greatest amount of sympathy for that Prime Minister, Mr. Chamberlain. Not only did he turn the other cheek to the enemy but he turned it several times. Certainly he must have suffered the greatest agony of humiliation when undergoing what he did. But in undergoing that, while thoughtlessly many people have said -that he gave away much that he should not have given away, for the time being at least he saved the world from a horrible slaughter.
Yesterday afternoon when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke, I heard him say that the danger was not past, a fact which I believe we all realize. Only the cool heads will be able to stave off the danger a little longer, and yet a little longer, until possibly the world may realize the utter madness of another holocaust such as those of us who are older went through between 1914 and 1918. There is nothing for a government to do but to do the best it can in times of such anxiety. Those of us who are not responsible can sit on the side lines and criticize. It is very easy to find fault; it is easy to criticize. But I sometimes wonder how much better we could have done ourselves. I doubt if there are many of us who would have done even as well. During the crisis the Yukon was deeply interested, dreading the thought of war. Yet at the same time every heart beat in unison with the empire and every person was willing to do as was done in the days of 1914, 1915 and 1916. If needs be, they were ready to answer the call of king and country.
Changing the subject very quickly, we come to the pleasant thought of the visit of Their Majesties, the King and Queen. In 1937 I had the privilege of suggesting to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) that silver coinage be issued by the government to

commemorate the coronation. Not for one moment do I intimate that the minister followed my suggestion. But the fact remains that silver coinage was issued, and among my few souvenirs I cherish the coin issued at that time, as well as the silver dollar issued at the time of the silver jubilee.
We see by the papers the government will again issue souvenirs by way of silver coinage and stamps. I am particularly interested in the issue of silver because in the Yukon there is a large territory in the Mayo district devoted to silver lead mining. As hon. members from British Columbia will no doubt point out, that province also is interested in silver mining, and anything that can be done to encourage our miners will surely be of infinite help to that class of people, upon whom many governments depend.
In the royal couple about to visit this country we have a fine example of manhood and womanhood in the British Empire. Suddenly these two people were called upon to fill a staggeringly difficult position. Neither one of them had trained deliberately to occupy a throne. Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth is a commoner, though of royal descent through the female line. The king was a prince occupying a secondary position. Yet in the twinkling of an eye those young people accepted a huge responsibility. No one in the world can say they have not filled the position thus far with grace and dignity not only to themselves but to the empire at large. Courageously and prayerfully they are carrying on. We owe them a great debt and our best efforts to make their lives happier and easier. They are coming to Canada and from one end of the country to the other every respect is to be shown them.
Unfortunately the Yukon is not to be visited by the royal couple, but I am free to say that Yukoners one and all feel a steadfast loyalty and fealty to- those young people who are carrying on so bravely and so well. Possibly they are fortunate in the example which has been set them by the late King George Y and his royal consort Queen- Mary for whom the world has the greatest affection. Although I was born and brought- up in the republic to the south of us, from girlhood I was trained by a grandmother who had strict old country ideas, and later by the sisters of the Holy Cross I was taught to look on England as-a shining example of what royalty could show to the rest of the world. That was taught, despite that conduct of England towards the colonies which made them rebel. Queen Victoria, later her son, then her grandson and then her great grandson have all been

The Address-Mrs. Black
familiar figures to me, both from reading and through conversation at home and at school. I have lived here now for forty years and have grown to realize what this country can be, what it has been and, pray God, what it will be for many years to come.
It is possible that the most interesting thing to us in the Yukon at the present time is the Alaska-Yukon highway. Many years ago the building of the road was advocated, and I well remember when Mr. Tolmie, the then premier of British Columbia, in the company of his ministers, took a trip as far as he could in northern British Columbia. My husband was appointed a member of the Canadian commission, and he now has in his office hundreds of photographs, surveys, letters and reports dealing with that road. I could give to the house a hundred reasons why the road should be built, and possibly I could give as many why it should not. If the road is built, I trust that men who know that northern country will be put in charge. It will be an enormously expensive work. The government of Canada cannot afford it, and certainly the government of British Columbia, debt-ridden as it is, cannot afford it.
We are told by the public men of the United States that that country wants this road for defence purposes. We have to face the fact that should- the United States be at war, Canada would be at war. We have to face the fact that if any untoward incident brings Canada into a war, the United States will be at war. That country could not stand by and see Canada fall. That would be impossible. She would not allow foreigners to touch Canadian territory any more than we would feel that we could allow foreigners to touch United States territory. The United States wants the road, and if the government is going to allow it to be built, I would urge that the United States be asked to pay every cent of the cost of building the road through Canadian territory, employing only Canadian labour and giving to Canada a free port of entry at Skagway. Some hon. members may smile at the mention of a free port of entry at Skagway, but we have a precedent. A free port of entry was allowed during the reign of Queen Victoria at Sault Ste. Marie and in the Gaspe.

speechtext: I am in favour of a free port.

speechtext:
I believe that was done in I860, but the permission was revoked after six years. At one time there was a Canadian customs office in Skagway. The stars and stripes and the union jack flew side by side. That was a great convenience, but unfortunately some one with more of what he thought was patriotism than brains objected to " that rag," as he called the union jack, flying in God's country. I was not a British subject at the time, but I stepped up to him and I said, " Another fool " 1 He looked at me and said, " That is like all you English women." I said, "As it happens I am the eighth generation bom and brought up in the United States." I told him that that had been done for the convenience of Yukoners going through United States territory. I told him that the United States would have to apologize, that Canada would have to accept the apology, but that the Yukoners would have to have their baggage and other possessions examined at the summit. So I suggest that if the road is built, it should be understood that we have a free port of entry at Skagway.
It is difficult for Alaskans and Yukoners to put up with the tariffs between the two countries when they pass from one country to the other. Perhaps this trade agreement of which we have heard so much will change conditions, but at any rate if the road comes to pass, as it probably will-the Hudson Bay railway came to pass-we should try to get the best bargain we possibly can. My confreres in the United States are good bargainers. I say that without any disrespect. I come from a family of down-east Yankees who made money selling wooden nutmegs. If they could do that then, I am sure they have not lost that ability at the present time.
When coming to the house many members display a spirit of optimism, while many others display a spirit of pessimism. We in the Yukon have been greatly favoured by not having the large numbers of unemployed that you have on the outside. A few drifters came in this summer, one or two of whom did not want to work. However, I must say that I believe I could count on the fingers of one hand the men who did not want work. One man came to me and said that he was tired of trying to get work. I asked him if he had tried pick-and-shovel work. When he told me he had not, I asked him what he had come there for. He said, "I heard you say that the Yukon was a place where every man could get a job." I said, "I may have said that, but what I meant was that every man who wanted a job could get a job provided he was willing to do gruelling, back-breaking work." I told him he could not get anything for nothing in that country. He leaned back and looked at me and said that I was a fine member. He told me, "The government has to take care of me or else send me out." It is not often that I lose my temper, but I did then. I used language that he understood. I am sure

The Address-Mrs. Black

you would ask me to retract that language, Mr. Speaker, if I used it here. I said to him, "Why don't you walk from here to Skagway?" He said, "How far?" I told him it was only about four hundred miles. He said, "What do you mean by insulting me?" I said, "My husband and my brother have walked that distance and they are much better men than you will be even though you live to be a thousand." He said, "This is no country for a white man to live in." Under the circumstances, I was forced to agree with him.
The Yukon is a good country; it is a cruel country; it is a kind country; it is a wicked country. It is a country that you can love; it is a country that you can hate, depending upon your attitude. I have lived there for forty years; I have travelled from one end of Canada to the other, as well as across the United States; I have travelled overseas; but I have never in my life seen a country that could thrill me as does the Yukon. We have our cruelties; we have our hardships; we have our glories, and we have our magnificent summers. We have our flowers, our vegetables, our gold and silver, but only when we work for them. If we come down here, it is because we have worked, not because we have sat back and folded our hands.
I wish that hon. members were more familiar with that country. Then, instead of smiling when I ask for a favour, instead of thinking that the Yukon wants all and gives nothing, they would remember the many men from that part of the country who have paid off the mortgages on their farms; they would remember the many men who served overseas during the great war. Out of a population of less than 5,000, over 500 men enlisted before conscription was brought in. All of us are ready to serve this country in time of peace and in time of war. We pray for the glory of peace and hope for its beauty.

Mr. Speaker, in my first attempt to speak the language of the majority in this house, may I crave your indulgence, and ask my colleagues not to be too severe in their criticism.
The hon. member for the Yukon (Mrs. Black) will undoubtedly forgive me if I do not follow her in her remarks. But I want to say that I am always very much interested in what she has to say to the house and also in the interest she takes in the far and cold country that she inhabits.
I also want to congratulate the proposer and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews), a newcomer in this house, has surely done credit

to himself and to his constituency; and the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier) has shown once more that he is well informed in politics, that he is a good debater, that he is a thorough bilinguist, and one for whose future his compatriots have great hopes.
As was so well said in the speech from the throne, every citizen of our country rejoices in the coming of our sovereigns to Canada this year. We Erench-Canadians are proud to say that we are not the ones least honoured by this visit. Might I suggest that when Their Majesties King George and Queen Elizabeth are in Ottawa, the capital city of Canada, we as the first civilized settlers in this country should have an official representative to express in our own language to their majesties our homage, our past and present loyalty to the crown, with the strength of our traditions and our true aspirations for the future.
Might I express on behalf of my compatriots and my constituents our wholehearted gratitude for the non-committal attitude taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his government during the dark days of the European crisis in 1938. It is, undoubtedly, similar steps that are conducive to the maintenance of peace in the world. Canada can be proud of the attitude of its Prime Minister and its government in that instance, and, by the way, of the cooperation that was given to the government by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Manion).
It is also refreshing to consider the friendship expressed to other nations by our government in the conclusion of trade agreements with other parts of the world, but principally at this moment with the United States of America. We are all sure that every part of our dominion will greatly benefit from that new trade agreement. The last trade agreement between the United States and Canada brought a great deal of comfort to our population, and we hope for still better consequences through the new regulations which are placed in the present trade agreement.
Here, I think, it would be only timely to suggest that special attention be given to trade possibilities with the countries of South America, where there is a population of eighty-five millions of people, who produce commodities which are not produced in our country and who necessarily buy commodities which are produced in the country we inhabit. Let us hope that goodwill will be the governing factor in all our relations with other

The Address-Mr. Bertrand (Prescott)
countries, and that this point of view will be always fully considered when questions of armaments and defence are under study. May I add that my compatriots dislike war; they have a very strong feeling against it, and they are not always ready to approve any move which looks like preparation for it.
Everyone regards with anxiety the unemployment problem in Canada. I do not hesitate to say that this is a very difficult problem, and that probably too much was said during the past year to the effect that it should be treated as a national question. I am not afraid to say in this house and elsewhere that this problem should be dealt with in all instances by the nearest competent body, by which I mean the municipality. Outside of large cities, almost every family is known intimately by the mayor, reeve, aldermen or councillors, or any one of them. May I then ask who is in a better position than they are to deal with these individual needs and these problems which arise in these different places? Instead of taking the matter away from them I would suggest rather that adequate assistance be given to those municipalities where the situation is the worst; it should not be removed from those who are best able to make the people understand that, after all, the state cannot give them a living for all time.
For this reason I am pleased to learn from the speech from the throne that a public works program will be undertaken by this government to face the situation, and also that laws will be made to help local work programs and local improvements. In making this statement may I venture to say that we should not fritter this program away by asking for problematical provincial guarantees when these works are done by the municipalities. The said guarantees have been given by some provinces and refused by others in the past year, and some municipalities which are positively in a good financial position are therefore denied the privilege of benefiting from the agencies to help unemployment in their , districts. If the necessity of a provincial guarantee is enforced, I am afraid the result will be that work will be done in places where the security is problematical and will be refused to municipalities where a great deal should be done by way of local improvements and that this would be justified to help the situation as regards unemployment through loans so granted for local improvements.
Passing to another item of the speech from the throne, I want to say that there are no more important works than the youth train-71492-7J
ing program. We are all satisfied to learm that it will be continued and enlarged. Youth' is the future of our country. Means should be taken to help each and every young man to improve his situation and to give him some help to learn some trade or craft so-that he may be able to make his own struggle in the development of the future of our country.
I wish now to make a few comments on the paragraph of the speech from the throne which reads:
In order to avert economic disaster to a large part of our population, my ministers, under the terms of the Wheat Board Act, approved, for the current crop year, an initial payment for wheat as recommended by the board.
In this paragraph I take the words, " a large part of our population," to mean the population of the prairie provinces. I hope it is unnecessary for me to give further explanations to convince anyone of the correctness of this interpretation. For a few months now we have seen all sorts of articles and propaganda concerning the difference in the situation as between eastern and western Canada, and when I speak of western Canada I mean the prairie provinces. Comparisons have been made in this propaganda on platforms and elsewhere. Not that I have any grudge against the guarantee of the price of wheat that was given to the west by the government, but if it can be given to the west my contention is that it can be given to other parts of the country .as well. When these provinces joined confederation, it was to be supposed that their administrations would increase their services in about the same ratio to population as other parts of Canada. Let me state that the cost of education in the prairie provinces has increased six times more than the increase in population, and the cost of public services has increased thirty times as fast as the Increase in population.
In the east it will be found that people managed to make both ends meet; this was done by economy and thrift. And may I say that the further east you go, the thriftier are the people. If anyone took the trouble to visit parts of the maritime provinces and see what the fishermen of that country live
} Mr. E. O. Bert.-and.]
upon, he must admit that they must be thrifty, and very thrifty. But many slices of the savings of the people of the east by thrift and economy were taken in taxes to help the prairie provinces in one way or another. I shall not undertake to state amounts so transferred or to state the help given to that part of Canada; but I do say that if in order to avert economic disaster in the western provinces it was necessary to fix a guaranteed price of eighty cents a bushel for No. 1 hard wheat f.o.b. Fort William, it is the opinion of the farmers of the east and of other parts of the country who have been realty battling with troubles and difficulties in the last few years, who were also hard hit by the crisis or by poor crops, that it is also necessary to fix and guarantee a reasonable price for commodities produced by the agricultural population in other parts of Canada, shall we say cheese, or butter, or potatoes, or maybe wheat, oats and barley, seed clover or timothy, or vegetables, and all commodities sold-may I draw attention to this proviso- sold at less than cost of production in this year or past years.
The farmers of my county strongly oppose price fixing by the state. They claim that this is something which governments should

The Address-Mr. Thompson
not undertake. They claim that it is far from Liberal policies. But if it is to be done, let it be done so as to do justice to farmers in all sections of the country. May I add, let it be done to do real justice to all classes of the population.
Let me end my remarks with one quotation from an address delivered by Premier Bracken of Manitoba as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of January 13, 1939, at page 6:
No large economic area of the country can for any length of time remain impoverished by failure of federal policies to secure markets and during this period be expected to meet its indebtedness, or be enthusiastic about national unity.
Of course this declaration is not made by anyone in the east. But if this declaration can apply to the difficulties of the farmers of the west, I say it is doubly applicable to the farmers of the east in the past year, and it is my plea on their behalf on this occasion.
In this great Canada of ours, for whose future we have great hopes, we want to build for this future on unity of population and an equal chance for all. I do not want to be too severe or to condemn what has been done; probably the situation was urgent, and it was practically impossible to do otherwise than fix this wheat price for the west for last year's crop; but let me say that to promote this unity and have our people feel that they are given an equal chance, I simply thought it my duty to raise my voice at this moment and to plead for just and fair treatment for all, to make this Canada of ours a place in which all will be satisfied to live and where people will feel that all are on exactly the same footing.

speechtext:
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my deep gratitude that Their Majesties the King and Queen have graciously consented to visit Canada. We have in this country our differences, political and otherwise; we have men of different races, different creeds, different nationalities, different outlook on life; but we all join together in honouring the same king. And I think this coming visit of their majesties will have a great unifying influence upon the Dominion of Canada, and that our people are looking forward to their visit with great pleasure as well as pride.
The speech from the throne is rather a meagre bill of fare to be presented to this house at a time when the masses of our people are looking for leadership; when they are looking for some national policies which will
give them a greater sense of economic security, and looking to be eased of their burden of unemployment and debt and taxes.
As to the proposal to increase the appropriation for defence, and particularly for air defence, I have no criticism to offer, so long as the contracts for the material required shall be honestly awarded and that precautions are taken to see that private individuals do not make undue profits out of them. The Canadian people at the present time are in no mood to countenance any further Bren gun contracts. The effectiveness of the proposal to form a defence purchasing board will depend entirely upon its personnel. If this government continues to do as it has done in the past, and to appoint political partisans as a reward for services rendered, this board will be nothing more or less than just another of this government's royal commissions that have been of no effect.
Unemployment, debt and taxes are the nightmares that disturb the peace of every thoughtful citizen in Canada; yet in the speech from the throne no mention is made of either our debt or our burden of taxation. Nor is any solution offered for our unemployment problem, nor any redress for the men and women who have been forced on relief by the policies adopted by this government, by their injurious trade agreements and by their continual tariff tampering. During the campaign of 1935 we remember with what eloquence the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-and he is an eloquent man-cried from one end of this country to the other that unemployment was Canada's most urgent national problem; that poverty and adversity, want and misery, were the enemies which Liberalism would seek to banish from this land. Further he said, " We take up at once, as our supreme task, an endeavour to end poverty in the midst of plenty." He also promised that the government would practise economy in the conduct of public affairs and that credit would be issued in terms of national need.
With all the eloquence at Ins command the right hon. gentleman used such beautiful phraseology and enunciated such high ideals, but where are the results? After every promise made by the right hon. gentleman during the last campaign can be written the word failure, dismal failure. We find that the Canadian Welfare Council, after a thorough investigation of the whole situation in Canada, said that no fundamental attack upon the serious national ills which have occasioned these heavy expenditures had been taken by the present government. That is an expression of opinion by a non-partisan organization
The Address-Mr. Thompson

in regard to what has taken place in the last three years. We have spent $900,000,000 and we are no better off than when we started. There is no improvement to-day.
It is quite true, Mr. Speaker, that the former right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) made promises in 1930. He said he would end unemployment or perish in the attempt, but of the right hon. gentleman and the government of that day it must be said that they did introduce those principles and policies which under normal conditions would have brought prosperity to this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite forget that from 1930 to 1935 the government of the day was piloting this country through the greatest depression the world has ever seen. But the present government, in normal times, has failed to redeem the promises it made to the electorate. The commission on employment and the trade agreements which have been negotiated by this government, and which it hoped would bring great prosperity to this dominion, have not relieved our economic situation, and as I travel throughout Canada I find that the people are tired of the present physician and are crying aloud for a new doctor to heal their wounds, a new leader to bring them out of this wilderness.
Increased trade, world trade, as advocated by the present government, will never solve our unemployment problem. A nation that depends for its economic welfare and security upon its exports to foreign countries places in the hands of the foreign buyers the prosperity of its people; for it has absolutely no control over the markets to which it sends its goods. Industry and agriculture in this country are not enemies; they are partners in our development. Agriculture supplies the raw materials; industry supplies the manufactured articles, and they must work in cooperation. In future, industry, to a far greater extent than agriculture, must take up the slack of our unemployment. As farmers, we are producing a surplus of every food that can be profitably produced in Canada. We are not only feeding our own people; we are exporting large quantities of foodstuffs. But what about our manufactured articles, our machinery, our clothing and everything in the manufactured line? At least fifty per cent of it is being bought from foreign countries. We are sending our money out of this country instead of building up. markets for our farmers at home. After all, with the exception of wheat, we consume over ninety per cent of our agricultural products at home, and when we build up industry here we build up markets for the farmer. The greatest market the farmer has to-day consists of the men and women engaged in the industrial life IMr. Thompson.)
of this dominion, who are non-producers of agricultural products. When we build up industry we build up agriculture and the country prospers, but the very moment industry is at a low ebb we find our farmers in distress.
I represent a constituency in which there are many large textile mills. Between 1930 and 1935, when a Conservative government was in power, many of these mills ran day and night. What is the situation to-day? One of the largest mills in my riding is closed while several are running only part time. When I was home last weekend I was talking to the owner of a great mill, who told me that between 1930 and 1935 his mill ran day and night. To-day it is miming only three days a week, and his goods are not being sold but are being put in storehouses. He said,-" I am running my mill because I do not want to have my people go on relief, I am trying to retain my employees." The men and women who are getting relief to-day are not the people who are suffering the most. We have a class of people who are being employed only two or three days a week, who are earning just enough to keep body and soul together, and who are too proud to ask for relief. These are the people to whom my heart goes out.
In the county of Lanark there is one mill which is at present running day and night. That mill is manufacturing cloth from shoddy. I went to examine it the other day, and the proprietor told me he did not buy one pound of wool. It is a good looking cloth which he sells to the ready-to-wear clothing manufacturers who, in turn, produce cheap suits. The policies of this government have so reduced the purchasing power of the average person that he is not able to afford to buy a good suit of clothes. The mills making good cloth are idle, while this mill, turning out a cheap quality product, is running day and night. That is the condition in which we find industry.
The policies of the present government have not effectively dealt with unemployment, much less solved it. The situation is as it was when the government took office, unemployment is still Canada's greatest national problem. If we work together in unison, I believe there is not any problem concerning the whole country which cannot be solved by the combined effort of our Canadian people. But if we are divided we are lost.
A few years ago, prior to this government taking office, internal discord was a cloud on the sky no bigger than a man's hand; to-day it darkens the whole horizon and threatens the very foundation of our confederation.

The Address-Mr. Thompson
Canada is fast disintegrating into nine sovereign provinces. Where is the dream of the fathers of confederation of a great, united Canada? Where is the happy family of Liberal governments the Prime Minister predicted before the last election?
Reference was made in the speech from the throne to the Canada-Uuited States trade agreement which I shall not discuss at length at the present time. I trust I shall have an opportunity to make further observations when the agreement is before the house.
The speech from the throne offers no relief to the already overburdened taxpayers of Canada. We cannot continue this process of pyramiding our national debt and yearly adding millions of dollars of deficits. If we do so continue a huge debt will be left as a burden on our children and our children's children. Are we going to pass this country on in that condition to those who will come after us? That is not the way in which we received it from our forefathers, and it is up to us to see that we pass it on without unduly hampering those who will come after us. Posterity will have enough problems of its own to solve without the people of this day heaping ours upon their backs. Let us bear our own burdens. The eleven million people in Canada are to-day carrying almost all the taxation they are able to bear. I should like to see it made compulsory for every government to live within its means and to balance its budgets or, failing that, to be placed in a position, except in case of war, where it would be obliged to resign and go back to the people.
The speech from the throne was replete with beautiful phrases which meant anything or nothing, but which were characteristic of the present do-nothing government. I was surprised last evening as I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) twitting the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Manion) with lack of patriotism. When the great war broke out, there were in Canada people in the prime of their lives who had no families and who could have rendered good service to then-country, but instead of that they slipped quietly across the border into the United States and secured good positions. Following the war they came back quietly, when they thought all was quiet on the western front. Compare that, I say, with the record of the Leader of the Opposition. When war was declared, he was a married man with a family of small children and with one of the largest medical practices in central Canada. He was rapidly becoming one of the most promising surgeons in Ontario. What had he to leave? He left his wife, his family and
his business, donned the king's uniform and for three years offered his life in the defence of Canada. It ill becomes the Prime Minister or any other man to twit the present leader of the Conservative party with lack of patriotism.
I ask in all sincerity: Whither is the Prime Minister leading Canada? Whither are we bound?

speechtext:
His first act after the
election of 1935 was to hie himself to Washington and, while there, sign a trade agreement which the leader of the former government (Mr. Bennett) had refused to sign because, big business man as he was, he realized that its provisions were detrimental to the best interests of the Canadian people. What has happened since then? Since that trade agreement became effective, our exports to the United States have fallen off every year and our imports have increased by millions of dollars. The former leader of the Conservative party foresaw that.
Last year, 1938, the Prime Minister sent a few civil servants to Washington, and, while there, they negotiated a trade agreement bargaining away Canada's birthright for a mess of pottage. In 1932, when the trade agreements were signed in Ottawa, my former leader called a special meeting of parliament and placed the agreements before it for en-dorsation prior to their becoming effective. He did not ignore parliament or the elected members of the house. What about later trade agreements? In 1935 the present government signed a trade agreement on the first day of January and called parliament together a few weeks later. Then the government's supporters were jumping up like a lot of jacks-in-the-box voting for something which had been in effect before being presented to parliament. What about the trade agreement which was signed recently? It became effective on January 1, 1939, and parliament was called on January 12. Again members of the House of Commons have been utterly ignored. Where is responsible government going? Where is our much boasted democracy? We have a government that has been governing this country without paying proper respect to the members of this house. We have had orders in council. We have had royal commissions in connection with which many of their Liberal lawyer friends were paid daily fees that they could^ not possibly earn in months in their own business. Some of them have drawn in fees during the last three years between $30,000 and

The Address-Mr. Thompson
$40,000 from the public treasury of this country to produce reports similar to the one the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot) threw on the floor of the house last session stating it was fit only for the waste-paper basket. That is how hundreds of, thousands of dollars of the money of the taxpayers of Canada has been spent in the last few years.
What this country needs, and needs in the worst way, is a public conscience. We must arouse a public conscience in the electorate. If a government have been honestly and wisely discharging the duties of their office; it they have been fulfilling the promises made to the people, then I say that they have every right to be returned to office. If they have not, then the people should tell them so with no uncertain sound. We have been prone to form ourselves into political camps. We are too ready lo go out and fight for our side as we used to do in school when playing football, lacrosse or some other game. We have been fighting for our own side. Let us awaken in this country a public conscience so that any government, I care not what it may be, will be afraid to go back to a discriminate electorate when they have not faithfully, honestly, and wisely discharged the duties of their office.
I do not wish to speak at any further length at the present time, but I think we should cease harping on the past. I know that the Conservative party has nothing to regret in that regard. That party has had a glorious past in Canada. It has been associated with the development of this country and it has a record that we are proud to bring forward. But let us live for the present and for the future. That is all that matters. Let us like business men face the problems that confront Canada. Let us cease this party strife. No grain is ground by the water that passed by the mill yesterday.
