speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member from Manitoba I was proud of the performance of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. After three years of association with him in this house I was prepared for the eloquent speech of the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier). This is the first time I have risen in my place this session, and I should like to say to the leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Manion) in this house that as a western Liberal I was delighted over his elevation to his present position.

But it is of more serious things that I would speak. The people of Winnipeg South rejoiced to learn of the visit of their majesties. I can say on behalf of the people of that city that when that visit does occur, their majesties will indeed receive a royal welcome.
Since this house met last, the world has walked in the valley of the great shadow, and it continues. I think every hon. member and every person in the country are delighted over the fact that for the moment at any rate the dark clouds have lifted. But the whole experience has left a bitter taste in the mouths of many of us. We have deep apprehension because we have had a glimpse of ourselves as people. To say the least, this has been disconcerting. The conclusion has been forced upon many of us that after twenty years we have learned nothing. Diplomacy as practised in the world to-day is not something that decent people can view with any degree of complacency. When we view the welter of hypocrisy, timidity, treason and greed, it is poor consolation to remember that a year ago most of what has happened -was predictable and was predicted in this house. Then we might have said as -was said in the sixteenth century, I think by John Selden:	.
Thou little thinkest what a little foolery governs the world.
There is little profit in evaluating the past unless we are to learn from our observations, unless we can hope to use the lessons of the past as a guide in the future. Here at the beginning of a new session we had better realize again that yesterday is gone, that to-morrow never comes, and that to-day waits while we hold post-mortems on yesterday or build fanciful structures on the sands of to-morrow.
I think if an object lesson were needed by members of this house, this new session provides an excellent one in the passing from this chamber of the previous leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). We have watched him in recent years fighting a rearguard action inspired by a political philosophy that may never again become invigorated in Canada. He made the assumption of infallibility seem more impressive than truth. He was a product of an age and generation when every Canadian boy knew that if he minded his own business, worked hard and saved his money, he might one day make a million dollars and be Prime Minister of Canada. The last great exponent of that theory having accomplished

The Address-Mr. Mutch
both, we can now turn the page and gaze on the reality of the opportunities of youth in Canada in 1939.
The last three years have been years of accomplishment. For what has been done we shall have no lack of praise and explanation, of criticism and condemnation. Neither my tongue nor my temper is suited to the task of flattery. Even honest praise, well merited, must for me be tempered by the meaures of opportunity and need. First, have we done that which was crying out to be done? Second, have we done all we might have done? I think it was Rousseau who envisioned men as being born free and equal and everywhere in chains. To-day, of freedom and equality we have still precious little. Unhappily only a few voices are raised to cry out against this condition, and man is everywhere in chains. Even in Canada, where as yet we keep the outward and visible emblems of liberty, the substance is disappearing. We have given too little thought to the preservation of our heritage, forgetting the truism that eternal vigilance is the price of liberty.
I find the most disconcerting evidence of that in the youth of the world. Irreverence, independence, intolerance, is the natural heritage of youth. Do we find it? We do not. I suggest that we find indifference, dependence and docility making great inroads into the spirit of youth. My generation has been called the lost generation. We were those who were young in the war. That was tragedy, but a worse tragedy threatens another generation who may yet be called the legion of the damned. Damned to what and by what? Obviously I do not mean that they are damned morally, spiritually or for the hereafter, but I do suggest that it will take superhuman effort to salvage them economically, at least from a condition of affairs not of their own making. They are a generation in economic chains and their political liberty is, I submit, threatened. They ask us what can be done. For my part I answer-honestly, as youth ought to be answered-in so far as their immediate economic liberation is concerned I do not know what anyone can do that they cannot do for themselves. But I think that there devolves upon us in this house a duty to preserve, for them particularly, the political liberties which they might in their extremity be tempted to forego. I am not a revolutionary. Time was when perhaps I was, but now I would be prepared to build before I would be willing to tear down. I suggest that we have not exhausted the avenues of approach to work. Although I have nothing but praise for the
long term policies of the present administration, I suggest that a wasting generation cannot afford to wait.
We have not examined to my satisfaction the possibilities of making industry bear its own burden. It is nonsense to say that they can pay no more. They are bearing the burden and adding to it by the wasteful systems of exploitation of labour which I am sorry to say are current in the country to-day. They are bearing the burden and adding to it. Labour pools do exist in this country; they are increasing at the present time, and this particular evil is getting by unnoticed in the guise of seasonal unemployment.
What do we need? What is our Canadian objective for youth, for mankind? Do we adopt the materialistic Huey Long concept of a radio and a two-car garage for every home, or do we seek some measure of competence, a reasonable hope of security in labour, and a world at peace where men and women work out their destiny with some relationship between ability and reward? When this or any other government is criticized as a do-nothing government, almost always the foremost critics are those who are wailing because the government has done nothing for the critic or the critic's business or the interests that are lying near and dear to the heart of the critic. Most of those who are contributing to the undermining of our democratic order proceed selfishly and without reckoning the cost. Most of those whether they are young or old, who decry governments, criticize politicians or damn the system, are howling because in some way they hoped to live off the taxpayers and have not succeeded. Is it not time that we in Canada faced up to this attitude? Why should governments do anything for the individual? What is the function of government? What are the oft orated rights of youth? Is not this the function of government and the main right of youth, that the government should see that every youth has a chance to exercise his talents within the range of opportunity available? Because too many youths desire to be doctors, should the government poison people to bring them patients; or because there is a desire on the part of too many people to be architects, must we go on forever and ever building government buildings in order to employ them?
We have a youth problem in western Canada. There is nothing, new about youth problems, but they are new to us in the west. Three decades ago the youth problem was

The Address-Mr. Mutch

an eastern problem, easily solved because the frontiers of the west were calling to the second and third and fourth sons of back concession farmers, presenting an opportunity which has departed from this country at the present time. The young men of the east, more than eastern dollars, builded western Canada, and the youth of the west too was quickly absorbed in an ever-expanding economy. To-day there is no new frontier other than the north. Truly as yet the limits of northern development are far from being reached, but it has also little appeal to many of a generation who have been educated to "ask, and it shall be given unto you." I do not blame them. You cannot blame them; but we can and we should blame ourselves, and in my opinion it is time to stop.
Whenever the largesse demanded by the indigent is threatened, the venerable leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth) thunders in effect that to those who ask for bread we offer a stone. I ask, cannot discussion ever be honest? The choice is wider than to give bread or a stone. Why not recognize the fact that organized society is being blackjacked into providing for some at least who insist on pointing their lives in one particular direction or else sit tight and let someone else do it. We have a youth problem in western Canada. During the civic elections in Winnipeg I heard a young man say, and I took down his words, "I spent years in preparing myself for a responsible position." He should have prepared himself for a job. Responsibility comes with experience, not with education. Education should speed up the process.
The economy of the west is still agricultural, and no economy can provide for youth which plans to live off it rather than in it. In Winnipeg the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has been loud in its condemnation of the farm placement scheme. Natural^. That party has thrived by organizing the discontented, the dissatisfied and those ever ready to follow any glimmer that promises to lessen their responsibility for their own existence. That party has no interest in an agricultural society save to exploit the farmer's real or fancied grievances for their own political advantage. That party is the real parasitic, political growth, battening on misery and discontent. Please bear in mind that I deliberately discriminate between my friends of the labour party and their political associates in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation.

Even in the so-called normal days between 1922 and 1930 young Canadians left Canada at the rate of about fifty thousand a year. Why? Who were they? Hon. members know the answers. Were they farmers, miners, fishermen, lumbermen? In the main, no. Few of them were primary producers. Many of them were educated beyond their opportunity, or so it seemed to them. They were definitely young people who could not, or would not, fit into the Canadian economy and could not live off it. And at that time we did not take care of them if they could not live off it. I am told that in one year every member of a western graduating engineering class went to the United States or to South America.
The last Conservative government while in opposition in these years wailed incessantly because we were losing these exotic blooms from our educational hothouse. In power the same party dammed up every possible avenue of approach to a job in Canada by stifling our trade and so smothering our productive industries. To-day more youths are finding work. But who are they? They are mainly the newest recruits to the ranks of youth. The boy who was too young for a job ten years ago is now refused the same job because he is too old. The generation from twenty-five to thirty-five has to be considered in Canadian economy.
Our problems are not all insoluble. Honest facing of them will pave the way to some solutions. Clearly there is no obligation to provide for employment in any particular job or profession. There is perhaps an obligation to render labour as fluid and mobile as possible. Establishment of the projected dominion government employment agencies will clearly help in that direction. I, regret that no mention is made of it in the speech from the throne. If we had it, no excuse would need to be accepted. If we are to accept the theory that every man has a claim on the state for his living, then the state will ultimately have to say how he shall earn it and where. Is that what youth wants? Ultimately perhaps it offers a measure of security, but at the price of liberty. The only countries in the world without a youth problem to-day are those where youth has been enlisted in state organizations or those which are at war. The story of those states is on every front page. Is that the best the world has to offer youth? Mr. Speaker, there are those of us who do not think so. There are those of us who still contend that there is no economic necessity for the degradation of another generation of mankind. I could not help but regret that the

The Address-Mr. Mutch
leader of the opposition was more anxious to prove conditions were worse than formerly than to suggest a remedy.
Those of us who hold this view ask of our government two things, both of them within their power to do. They are these: First, that they stand four-square for peace, not for the hope of peace, not for peace if the price is not high, but for peace that is absolute. How can they do so? We believe that this and any government can foster peace and security by being well informed and by backing reliable information, by being always on the side, not of sentimentalism, not necessarily of nationalism, but, on the highest of all grounds, of morality, the expression of which is justice. Paradoxically, it is possible that justice can be done only by force, but our government must know; they must not be swayed by hysteria, emotionalism, sentimentalism, or business expediency. When we know, then we can act. When we know, we must not count the cost because, secondly, we believe that the cost of failure to restore confidence and friendly relations in the world is ultimately either a war which will eliminate western civilization as we know it, or alternatively the complete break-down of world trade with the inevitable result of starvation in a world of plenty and an equally inevitable world revolution.
Fear holds the world in its thrall. We ask our government to join in with each and all who will contribute in any degree to the reestablishment of good relations among men.
We are proud that our government has been a party to the recent tripartite trade agreements. The immediate economic results can be left to consequences. Those who believe as I do are confident that the results will be good.
But, sir, some of us are more impressed with the political significance of the trade agreements. We see the dawn of a realization that no nation can live to itself alone. We see the faces of the two greatest creditor nations turned to the sunlight of freer trade and better relations with the world. We rejoice that the ramparts of the Ottawa agreements have been breached. We hope that they may crumble to the inglorious dust whence they came. Born of fear, they throve to engender hate. For the mirage of momentary advantage we conspired with our commonwealth associates to encourage the rabid nationalistic orgy which is the greatest threat to the world.
We ask our government not to be too modest. Let them proclaim to all who will hear that we are not prepared to let a generation of Canadians perish because we must wait until mightier powers show us the way to renewed willingness to do business.
The Prime Minister's grandfather had a vision of a great opportunity and a great duty. The man was matched with the hour. How often in the years of his distinguished service to his country must my leader have hoped for this opportunity to match his talents with the nation's need. He is a man of peace. He is a man whose imagination and sympathy have kept him close to the realities of human experience. He is a man of deep conviction and the courage to fight when only a fight can meet the emergency.
Here, Mr. Speaker, is the emergency. Throughout the world all that he and we have held most dear is threatened. All around us a generation of Canadians are threatened with a living death. To-day, now, is the hour to strike! The walls of intolerance that have cramped the world have been breached- behind him sits a majority unparalleled in history. Around him sit men, good company in any fight-and, sir, there is time left. Time enough, to say as Holland has said for generations: Come, let us reason together, let us trade together. Time to say again to those fearful nations of the world, let us help you to help us. We have made a grand beginning; we dare not falter now.
Two thousand millions of people in the world need bread, motor cars, machinery, lumber and iron, paper, pulp, everything that we have to sell. Two thousand millions of people await only some way to pay in order to buy all those commodities which go to make possible the higher standards of living which man to-day in every comer of the world desires. Did I say, "only"? Alas, that is but half true- other restrictions do exist, but we can do more to break down the barriers. Many of our business men lack the imagination to visualize their opportunity. Their employees tremble for fear of losing a precarious living-failing to to see the possibilities of expansion. Motor car manufacturers, for example, shudder lest they lose a part of a two or three million market and fail to see the possibilities of a seventy million market. They try to sell us motor cars on the basis of the number of eggs they eat, or apples, or fish, while the parent companies, located in the United States where they have no competition, spend their advertising dollars trying to persuade United States consumers to let down the bars against foreign imports, realizing full well that, if they do, more United States cars will be exported.
Some misguided farmers turn to a plea for permanent price protection when they
71492-8J
The Address-Mr. Mutch

should be stiffening the determination of our government to trade our way into the markets of the world.
Professional calamity howlers urge restricted production in a .world that is a potential consumer of the maximum of production. Reduce acreage, bonus acreage, combine, restrict; their tongues and pens create a new Babel.
Professional agitators yelp for the redivision of wealth, for its restriction, for social dividends, for anything and everything except the opportunity to make wealth do its real job in the bettering of the living conditions of the world.
Our people realize that we have not come to the end of the road. The Canadian public will not forever be content to be cribbed, cabined and confined by a few chiselers with a good thing, by the fear of our industrialists or their employees or the lack of courage of legislative bodies.
Canadians cannot bring about the economic millennium, but we can have the courage to make a start-this government has done so. Is it too much to hope that we shall seize every opportunity, and make new ones, to go farther along the road to the economic salvation of ourselves and the world?
Dare we falter before the often expressed fear that by trading freely we may hurt our own pampered industries? "Oh, ye of little faith!" I, for one, am confident that Canadian brains and ingenuity, Canadian capital and Canadian labour can compete and hold their own. I believe they can. But, sir, if they cannot, let us count the cost. Must we contribute to the destruction of a generation of Canadian youth to protect such an industry, as would, by its failure, admit its incompetence and uneconomic establishment? The future is not devoid of hope. In seventy years England grew from seventeen millions to forty-six millions. We are ten millions and more. We have raw materials, power, geographic advantage, brains and brawn. Capital can be enticed from cover to promote the projects of a nation that is on the march, that knows where it is going.
Leadership is essential. Since business does not give it, parliament must. Courage is needed-the history of Canada is the story of undaunted courage. Faith is needed; for faith is the bed rock of confidence. We have all faltered in these last ten years. We need a touch of evangelical fervour in our attitude toward our problems.
We Canadians need to consider our political and social creed. May I give you mine? I believe in Canada, in her vast resources,
IMr. Mutch.]
and in the courage and ability of her sons and daughters. I believe in my neighbours, in the duty I owe them, and in the brotherhood of man. I believe that the peoples of the world have a right to a decent livelihood, and that this is possible with advantage to all. I believe that "fair exchange is no robbery," and that in peace and better trade relations lies the economic salvation of the world.	,
To this end we have made progress. But I come again to the need of the moment. May I say that in this I am motivated by a sincere desire to see immediate succour for those young people for whom I plead. For myself I can wait for the long pull; or, if I cannot, the great constituency which I represent has come through greater adversity than my departure from the scene would entail. At this moment the greatest reclamation problem in Canada is a human one, and its slogan and watchword is, Save our sons and daughters. The speech from the throne recognizes the need and makes it known that something more is to be done. May I reiterate what I have said every session since I came to this house, that the problem has become- indeed to my mind it always was-a federal one. I am not critical of proposals which have not yet been explained, but I warn the house that the municipalities where the need is greatest are broke. Let this government assume full responsibility for employable unemployed on aid; then perhaps with this government's cooperation the municipalities may be able to cope with the problem of those employable unemployed not on aid, among them our youth. I am not fool enough to imagine that any government can by legislative act or series of acts end unemployment. I do not believe that our banks or financial system are either the bulwark or the bugaboo of our existence. We have put on money the emphasis that we should have put on morality; we examine coinage when we should probe conscience.
I would not fool around with the British North America Act for five minutes. In time of war governments assume extraordinary powers. Well, this is a struggle for survival. What if it beats a ministry, if it saves a generation? I have boasted that I know of no hon. member in this house who does not wrestle with all the earnestness and ability at his command to find a way out for our people. The sharpest-tongued partisan in this house would wear the same uniform as the rest of us to defend our homes. Are our homes more important than the flesh and blood within them? Can we not either abolish or

The Address-Mr. Graydon
ignore these restrictions which hamstring the honest desire of every member, and get on with the job that has to be done? Then, if it is still necessary, we can let the lawyers argue the legality afterwards. If we can do that, then perhaps Canada-loving, Canada-serving legislators, federal, provincial and municipal, may be able to effect an approach to the settlement of the problems of our people, which is the honest desire of every hon. member of this house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At the outset of my remarks to-night I should like to pay a very well deserved tribute to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I was particularly taken with the splendid way in which the task assigned to these hon. members was discharged. The mover of the address (Mr. Matthews), a new man in the house, received the kind of welcome that this house is accustomed so generously to give. The seconder of the address (Mr. Chevrier), whom I have the privilege and honour of calling a very close friend, impressed, I think, every hon. member present not only with his sincerity and earnestness but also with the great facility with which he spoke the two languages in his address. Such men in public life do much to promote national unity in its widest and broadest sense. Therefore I congratulate both these hon. members.
I should also like to echo the widespread and general feeling of keen appreciation and eager expectancy so evident throughout the dominion in regard to the coming visit of Their Majesties the King and Queen. During the course of this debate many allusions have been made to that visit. The house may well spend considerable time in emphasizing the importance to Canada of the visit of these prominent personalities in world affairs. In these days of international unrest, and sometimes, perhaps, internal unrest, it is a very fine thing for Canada to experience the visit of our monarch and his consort. I am sure that throughout Canada all citizens will be vying with one another in an earnest and sincere effort to give to the king and queen one of the most spontaneous and affectionate welcomes that any monarch or ruler has ever received in the history of the world. I look for nothing less than that as far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned.
Also I want to congratulate the committee in charge of arrangements. These arrangements may not always meet with the approval of every hon. member, but with a fine regard for the king's wishes the itinerary does provide that their majesties pass through the
county of Peel. I want to thank the committee for the privilege and honour bestowed; upon our county in arranging that their majesties pass through that admittedly attractive part of this dominion.
It was appropriate that the speech from the throne should refer to the disturbed international situation. But it omitted to refer to the determined feeling which existed during that September crisis, and which was so prominently exhibited throughout the whole dominion ; I refer to that feeling of loyalty and patriotism to the British Empire. I should like to have seen in the speech from the throne some reference made to the fact stated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) just last evening, that when Great Britain is at war Canada also is at war. I was glad to hear him say that. If we are bold enough to say that ordinarily in this country, surely it is not too much to ask this government to include at this time a paragraph to that effect in the speech from the throne.
Then we have in the speech from the throne reference to a new defence purchasing board. Throughout the dominion, so far as I have been able to discover, there is not much feeling in favour of either commissions or boards. But if this board should be a strictly nonpartisan and non-political organization, perhaps it will not meet with so much criticism. But here again this government is delegating its administrative duties to another commission. Whether you call it a board or a commission, it is still the same type of organization against which many people in the dominion to-day rebel strongly. I am hoping that this board shall not be just another spending body, or as expensive as other commissions which have preceded it, because a great many people in Canada, a majority of them I think, to-day are searching for means to reduce the cost of government and the burden of taxation generally.
In the speech from the throne much stress is laid upon the question of trade agreements. That is only natural. At the commencement of my remarks in regard to trade agreements may I say that I should like to see matters such as this treated in this House of Commons with a fine balance of common sense and some idea of the proportion of things. In dealing with such questions-* and I know there must have been sins committed on all sides of the house from time to time in connection with matters of this kind-let us not be guilty of over-emphasis in offering criticism with respect to agreements of this kind which have not been long
The Address-Mr. Graydon

in operation, and on the other hand let us not make extravagant and reckless claims in regard to what the agreements will do. Surely it must be apparent to most hon. members, as it must be to the man on the street and the man on the farm, that when someone says these agreements are going to be great factors in international peace for the future, there is quite a dash of colour added. I would not for a moment suggest that agreements such as these may not have some bearing on questions such as peace, but so far as we in Canada are concerned, we as members have a trust and this government has a trust for the Canadian people. We must never lose sight of the fact that we are trustees for the people of this country, and before this government loses itself in a cloud of international understanding it must be sure that everything is well on the ground below. To me, Mr. Speaker, that seems to be one of the cardinal principles on which we must proceed to deal with the pros and cons of an agreement such as this. I do not believe Great Britain would ask, let alone permit, this dominion to jeopardize its interests in behalf of anything so fantastic as the suggestion that has come from some quarters that this agreement means the binding together of three great portions of the Anglo-Saxon world.
It is not difficult, of course, to recall the glowing hopes which were expressed some three years ago. I remember so well the supporters of the government suggesting that the agreement of 1936 was going to do- what? Well, it was to be a blow at economic nationalism; it was to encourage greater international understanding; it was to be a great benefit to agriculture, to business and to industry in general. Let us hurriedly examine what has happened with regard to the lesson in international understanding which the agreement of 1936 was supposed to teach.
1 would be the las.t one in this chamber to -suggest that this agreement was the cause of what happened; but when an hon. member suggests in this house that the agreement of 1936 was to be a great step towards a broader international understanding and a way to peace, perhaps I may be excused for very humbly and quietly pointing out that since that agreement went into effect, in 1936, there has been scarcely a moment when the tension has not become greater, until we bad the crisis of September last when an armed holocaust almost resulted. I give that illustration, Mr. Speaker, not with any desire to discredit the agreement as far as it went at that time, but merely to point
(Mr. Graydon.]
out the fallacies under which we may labour when we attempt to advance extravagant and reckless claims for agreements which have been scarcely entered into.
Let us look at this new agreement. May we not perhaps also remove a little of the colour from some of the statements we have heard in this house with regard to its part in international affairs? As yet I have not been able to come to the conclusion that it is going to be the means of ridding the world of the trouble with which it is confronted. I think most historians and students of foreign affairs will agree that our troubles in this world have deeper roots than the mere question of changing some of the items in the tariff schedules of the Dominion of Canada.
Let us look at the benefits which came from the 1936 agreement, so far as our people were concerned, leaving aside for the moment the lesson in international understanding to which I have just referred. Before that agreement came into operation, the 'balance of trade between the two countries was in favour of Canada. I am sure there will be plenty of hon. members who will say that the balance of trade is a worn-out theory; but in spite of that I should like to place upon Hansard the manner in which the trade balance was reversed, for the benefit of those who still cling to the theory that perhaps, after all, there is something in the balance of trade as far as a country is concerned. Canada, a country of eleven million people, bought from the United States last year goods to the value of $487,000,000. During the same period we sold to that country goods to the value of only $423,000,000, leaving an adverse balance of trade amounting to $64,000,000. Before the agreements were entered into, as I said before, we had a balance of trade in our favour in our trading relations with the republic to the south.
Let us consider fresh fruits and vegetables, in which I am particularly interested. In 1935, before the agreement went into operation, we imported approximately $13,000,000 worth of fresh fruits and vegetables. In 1938, after the agreement had been in operation for three years, we imported no less than $17,500,000 worth, or an increase of 35 per cent. Someone may ask, " Well, how did the agreement work"? I would not suggest that any public speaker supporting that agreement should go into any area where these fresh fruits and vegetables are produced; I am doubtful as to the welcome he might receive from some of those people.
But we must not confine ourselves entirely to that particular branch of agriculture in this country. Taking the figures for 1935 and 1938, covering the periods both before and after the

The Address-Mr. Graydon
1936 agreement, I find that there was some little appreciation in the price of cattle. On the other hand, the general price level of field crops and dairy products dropped to extremely low levels in the interval. In other words, the glowing and extravagant claims made for the old agreement were not, in all instances, substantiated by the results. Of course it must have helped some lines of business, but undoubtedly it also harmed others. So I think it would be a bold man indeed who would rise in this chamber to-night and say that the old agreement resulted in any overwhelming business recovery in the Dominion of Canada.
This subject of agriculture is very near to me, and perhaps hon. gentlemen will excuse the constant references to this question by one who represents a rural area, as I do. After all, however, there is something about the condition of agriculture that some people who come from urban sections seem to fail to appreciate. I was disappointed, yes, I was discouraged to find that the speech from the throne contains nothing that looks like a forthright, vigorous or aggressive plan for the rehabilitation of agriculture in Canada. It has been said many times that national agriculture in this dominion provides the best barometer of business conditions. I agree with that statement, and would couple with agriculture the condition of the working man. Those of us who represent constituencies where eastern agriculture is carried on at its best are deeply concerned. May I point out that no one is raising his voice in regard to the reasonable alleviation of the distressed condition of western agriculture. We realize that, after all, we cannot think in Canada simply as "I"; we must think as " we," because when we speak of one part of Canada we think of it all. May I point out, however, that this year eastern agriculture has experienced great hardships and low price levels, and many farmers in eastern Canada feel that perhaps the eastern end of agriculture ought to have some measure of rehabilitation too.
Last year I listened to an eloquent exposition of agriculture delivered by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) whom I see in his seat to-night. He pleaded with the government for assistance in promoting and arranging a market in the United Kingdom for Canadian chilled beef. There are many practical farmers in Canada who feel that in England we have a market of consumers, a great market where there is a heavy demand for high grade products of agriculture. One cannot wonder when he hears the farming population of Canada crying out for real opportunities to sell beef and
bacon in the British isles. I should like to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) begin to-night on a program of rehabilitation, so far as agriculture is concerned, and provide for the farmers of Canada a market in Great Britain for bacon and chilled beef. It always seems to me-and perhaps I am wrong in my premise-that we lay too much stress upon the market in the United States. We lay stress upon a market which is not alone a consumer's market but a market which has close to it competitive farmer producers who compete every day with our products sent in. On the other hand in the great British market that is not so to the same extent. The government is losing sight of the principles and policies which will help the farming population of Canada, and should make some aggressive and vigorous move to capture the market for bacon and beef in the British isles as quickly as it can be done.
One hears a great deal of talk about agriculture being the backbone of the country. I do not mind so much hearing a farmer make that statement, but I do not like to hear anyone who has not come from a farm or who does not understand farming, make it. Every member of the house must realize that the farmer-and I speak more particularly of the eastern farmer with whose conditions I am more familiar-is to-day caught between low prices and high overhead. I believe most practical farmers realize that this is one of the greatest problems they face. A great basic industry such as farming cannot survive with the increasing overhead which seems to come with every improvement in farm machinery and farm conveniences, when prices are not proportionately higher than they were when general overhead was much lower.
The prosperity of the farmer is reflected, in good times or bad, upon every class of person in Canada. It is the nation's business barometer; let us make no mistake about that. During the discussion of the trade agreements we shall hear about the prospective benefits which will accrue to the farmers, particularly in connection with cattle and milk. I do not wish in any way to detract from the glowing picture which has been painted. I should not like to spoil a good picture, even one painted by a Liberal government. On the other hand, with great respect I should like to point out that with relation to cattle weighing over 700 pounds the duty has been cut one-half cent per pound. But our farmers are still faced with a quota which prevents them from shipping into the United States and taking advantage of the entire market,
The Address-Mr. Gray don

so far as the sale of their cattle is concerned. I have made some calculations-I do not know whether they are correct-but they seem to indicate that even under the new agreement we can ship only one and one-quarter per cent of the total number of cattle slaughtered in the United States in previous years. That is not very great consideration, to say the least. It seems to me the United States farmers have taken due precautions to see to it that they are not going to meet with very great competition in that regard. Then, the agreement restricts the entry of cattle to the extent of 60,000 for every quarter year, so that when the market is good over there in any particular season we are cut down to that 60,000, again protecting the United States farmer. Let us make a simple computation. If every twelve of our farm population were to pool their farm stock in any single year for export to the United States, they would be able to ship only one head of cattle weighing over 700 pounds. If we figure it out on another basis, actually only one in every twenty-six of our total cattle population in Canada comes within the restricted quota.
Then I ask hon. members to look at the situation with respect to milk. The rate of duty has been reduced on milk entering the United States to the extent only of a yearly quota of three million gallons. That would seem to be quite a bit of milk. However, I looked up the figures, and I found that three million gallons means only one gallon in every 570 produced every year in Canada, or four gallons for every farm in the dominion. These figures may sound fantastic, but may I point out that the milk production in the county of Peel, which I have the honour to represent, is no less than nine million gallons per year. We produce in that county three times as much as the government permits for the whole of Canada under the quota. I repeat that in that one county we produce three times as much milk as under the new agreement there may enter the United States under the lower tariff rate. I do not wish to criticize the government unduly, but I must say that they will have to pardon me if I say that this is not likely to revolutionize agriculture to say the least, and is not likely to put our dairy farmers and cattle breeders in the higher income tax brackets for the year 1939.
May I draw the attention of hon. members to one further important matter. In the town of Brampton, which is in my constituency, there are cut-flower producers, about whom I have spoken many times in the

house. We have been affected in that connection by a reduction of fifteen per cent in the duty on cut flowers coming into Canada. I must admit that a similar concession has been granted on the product entering the United States, but we must remember that climatic conditions in the two countries are entirely different. The cost of production in one country cannot be compared with the cost in the other. The result is that all we can do is to hope that this agreement will not work any serious hardship. A good many workmen in the cut-flower industry are not enjoying very prosperous times to-day, and I am hoping that this agreement will not work to their disadvantage.
There is one more injustice of which I should like the government to take cognizance. A sales tax of eight per cent is imposed on cut-flower sales, although no sales tax is imposed on the sale of ordinary agricu-tural commodities. The cut-flower industry must face competition from outside sources and from many growers who do not have to pay the sales tax, and I think this item might well be the subject of exemption when the next budget is brought down.
I am interested also in the boot and shoe business. In one of the towns in my riding great difficulty has been experienced because of "short time" schedules in this industry. While it is perhaps too early to forecast what will be the result of this trade agreement, I cannot see where it will help the men and women working in the shoe industry to take away their protection to the extent of even five per cent on goods entering from the United States, plus the elimination of the three per cent excise tax.
A change has been made in the preference granted on apples and other fruits entering the British market from Canada. I was hoping against hope that the British preference would not be changed by this agreement. We have built up a great export market for apples and other fruits, and since the empire agreements came into force there has been an increase in the prosperity of our fruit producers generally. But now part of the protection is being taken away from our fruit growers. The preference on the British market is to be reduced, and it is possible that as time goes on the United States producer will enter that market to the detriment of our growers. I also want to make as vigorous a protest as I can on behalf of the vegetable growers. Before 1936 the general tariff protection offered to these men amounted to thirty per cent. This has now been reduced to ten per cent

The Address-Mr. Gray don
under the general tariff, with further restrictions in connection with dumping duties.
I am speaking on behalf of these hard working men who are able to obtain only a small return from their labours in the vegetable industry. If there is going to be a progressive drop in the tariff by various agreements that this government may enter into, there will be eventually little left of this great industry. While I am discussing this matter I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he pay some attention to the recommendation I made last year to provide in his estimates for the furnishing of a proper statistical set-up in connection with fruits and vegetables. The vegetable growers of this country feel that they are penalized because of lack of statistical information. I believe the minister would be well advised to take this into consideration.
I want to make reference to the omission from the speech from the throne of any really vigorous policy with respect to the working man and his familj'. I do not make any apology for being the spokesman for the working man in the riding which I represent. One of the best lubricators of the machinery of business is the wage envelope of the working man who spends his money freely on the necessities of life. He provides business with the greatest impetus that it can possibly have. This government might well be criticized for not promoting any scheme to help the working man.
Let me now consider unemployment insurance. What a hackneyed word that has become throughout Canada. Nineteen years ago a great Liberal convention met in the city of Ottawa. That was the convention which elected the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as leader of the Liberal party. That convention solemnly nailed in the platform of the Liberal party the plank of unemployment insurance. Last night the Prime Minister made an eloquent address. He said that we are coming closer to unemployment insurance legislation. The time to have introduced that legislation was during the nine years from 1921 to 1930 when Liberalism was in power and when this country had a share of world prosperity. At that time there was more in the pay envelopes of the working man. We had not entered the depression, and we did not have the spending on public affairs that we have to-day. That was when the Liberal government should have brought in unemployment insurance legislation.
But it was left for the Conservative party to enact in 1935 the only measure of importance with respect to unemployment insurance that we have had since the days of confederation. That legislation was sent to the courts where it became a legislative wreck. To-night I heard a Liberal member, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch), state that he believed that policy of putting through unemployment insurance was one which should be pursued to-day, even by this government. The Conservative government answered when urgency and emergency called, and I think their legislation will always stand as a monument to their efforts to solve the problems of the working man. If this government will bring in a workable scheme of unemployment insurance, I am sure they will have the support of every hon. member and of every man and woman in the Dominion of Canada. All they have to do is to enact the legislation and see that that happy family of provinces which was spoken of before, is a reality. There should be some real measure of assistance for the working man of the dominion.
The hopes of the working man seem to be raised every year by some mention of unemployment insurance in the speech from the throne, but nothing is ever done. No longer than two weeks ago a working man said to me, "Will there be unemployment insurance after this year?" I said, "I think there will be, because there will be a Conservative government to give it to you the same as they did in 1935." He said, "I hope your party gives us a little more leadership and shows a little more aggressiveness than this government has done, because we do not want any more sit-down strikes' in Ottawa."
Not one thing was said in the speech from the throne with regard to the relief of real estate holders in the Dominion of Canada from the burden of taxation. It has been said at mayors' conventions; it has been stated from municipal platforms all across the dominion, that there is a need of easing the heavy burden of taxation on real estate. Along with the great majority of Canadians I believe that we must provide some policy to coax and persuade private capital once more to get into business. Governments are into business. They are into business sometimes too far, I believe. If we can reduce our taxes, cut down our overhead, show the people that we mean business in parliament instead of delays and promises, we shall once more get private capital into circulation in our business in this country, and the wheels of industry will turn and prosperity will be with us once more. I am in favour of a drastic reduction in governmental overhead throughout this country. Perhaps I need do

The Address-Mr. Graydon
no more than mention that, because the need for a pay-as-you-go policy in the dominion, as pointed out only a few moments ago by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson), is one of our crying needs. The county I represent is a representative county of Ontario, and in the last eight years we have not only paid as we have gone in the county of Peel, but reduced our debenture indebtedness by sixty per cent. Is it too much to ask the government of Canada to do what municipalities are already doing. This parliament should be giving a lead; the municipalities should be following only; the cart has gone before the horse much too long.
In closing, I wish to revert to a matter which was referred to yesterday. Throughout the country confidence in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has not been strengthened in recent times. One hears criticisms all over the land with regard to the control exercised over radio broadcasting in general. The idea of having to pay a radio licence fee of $2.50 still rankles in the minds of most people. May I offer a friendly piece of advice to the government of the day; they will be surprised at the extent to which public opinion in this dominion is rebelling against the payment of any kind of radio licence fee. That is one matter which ought to receive the careful and immediate attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) and the government as a whole. If we are to have some kind of radio control, it must be such as will have the confidence of the people generally, and it should not be associated in the minds of everyone with what they regard as an annoying nuisance tax.
In this country we have talked a good deal about national unity. Perhaps we have not reached the point of achieving what we should like to do in that direction, but if we are to have national unity it must be predicated upon aggressive and vigorous leadership in the dominion House of Commons. Instead of blaming all the provinces of the dominion for our troubles, let us analyze our own short-comings as a national legislative body and government. Let us provide in this country leadership which will lead, not merely jompromise and delay, leadership which will jompel every corner of Canada to think in terms of the nation as a whole. Our responsibility for the reconfederating of Canada has become greater in these days when jealous and eager foreign eyes are cast upon us. Let us measure up to the job we have before us and provide efficiency in government, virile and progressive leadership in administration,

and a strong national feeling of strength and unity before it becomes too late. That, in my opinion, is one of our tasks in parliament to-day.
